content: In industrialized countries, second-generation antipsychotics, also known as atypical antipsychotics, are commonly used as the first-line treatment for schizophrenia. However, there is ongoing debate regarding the differences in efficacy and tolerability among these medications. This review specifically examines how ziprasidone compares to other second-generation antipsychotics in terms of efficacy and tolerability for individuals with schizophrenia or schizophrenia-like psychoses. The review included nine randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with a total of 3,361 participants. A significant limitation of the studies was the high rate of premature discontinuation, with 59.1% of participants leaving the studies early. Comparisons were made between ziprasidone and other antipsychotics, including amisulpride, clozapine, olanzapine, quetiapine, and risperidone. Ziprasidone was found to be less acceptable as a treatment compared to olanzapine and risperidone. Specifically, participants were more likely to leave studies early for any reason when treated with ziprasidone compared to olanzapine (5 RCTs, 1,937 participants, relative risk [RR] 1.26, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.18 to 1.35, number needed to harm [NNH] 7) and risperidone (3 RCTs, 1,029 participants, RR 1.11, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.20, NNH 14). However, ziprasidone was not significantly less acceptable than other second-generation antipsychotics. In terms of efficacy, ziprasidone was less effective than amisulpride (1 RCT, 123 participants, RR 4.72, 95% CI 1.06 to 20.98, NNH 8), olanzapine (4 RCTs, 1,291 participants, mean difference [MD] in PANSS total score 8.32, 95% CI 5.64 to 10.99), and risperidone (3 RCTs, 1,016 participants, MD in PANSS total score 3.91, 95% CI 0.27 to 7.55). There were no significant differences in tolerability between ziprasidone and amisulpride or clozapine based on the limited data available. One notable advantage of ziprasidone was its lower likelihood of causing weight gain compared to olanzapine (5 RCTs, 1,659 participants, MD -3.82 kg, 95% CI -4.69 to -2.96), quetiapine (2 RCTs, 754 participants, RR 0.45, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.74), and risperidone (3 RCTs, 1,063 participants, RR 0.49, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.74). Ziprasidone was also associated with less cholesterol increase compared to olanzapine, quetiapine, and risperidone. However, ziprasidone was linked to slightly more extrapyramidal side effects compared to olanzapine (4 RCTs, 1,732 participants, RR 1.43, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.99). It also caused a greater increase in prolactin levels compared to quetiapine (2 RCTs, 754 participants, MD 4.77 ng/mL, 95% CI 1.37 to 8.16). On the other hand, ziprasidone was associated with fewer movement disorders (2 RCTs, 822 participants, RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.97) and less prolactin increase (2 RCTs, 767 participants, MD -21.97 ng/mL, 95% CI -27.34 to -16.60) compared to risperidone. It is important to note that the review included 254 citations awaiting classification, which may alter the conclusions once these studies are assessed. In conclusion, ziprasidone appears to be slightly less effective than amisulpride, olanzapine, and risperidone. Its primary advantage lies in its lower propensity to cause weight gain and related metabolic side effects. However, the high rate of participants discontinuing the studies early limits the reliability of these findings.
